steps.title: Resisting scratches
steps.text: Hardness is the resistance of a stone to scratching. A harder material scratches a softer one; the reverse is impossible. It is the first form of durability. A soft stone gets scratched, loses its polish and turns dull from being worn.

steps.title: The Mohs scale
steps.text: In 1812, the mineralogist Mohs ranked ten minerals from the softest to the hardest: talc (1), gypsum, calcite, fluorite, apatite, orthoclase, quartz (7), topaz, corundum (9) and diamond (10). It is a relative scale: it gives the order, not the gap. Each mineral scratches the ones before it. To find your bearings: a fingernail is about 2.5, glass and a knife blade 5.5, a steel file 6.5. And the dust in the air contains quartz (7): a softer gem gets scratched little by little.

steps.title: Absolute hardness
steps.text: The steps of the Mohs scale are not equal. Measured with an instrument, absolute hardness (for example the Knoop scale) shows the reality: from corundum (9) to diamond (10) there is only one step on the Mohs scale, but diamond is about three times harder. These figures are not used to recognize a stone, but they explain why only a diamond can cut another diamond.

steps.title: Hardness pencils
steps.text: To test a stone, the gemmologist uses hardness pencils: points of known hardness (5, 6, 7, 8...). The points are drawn across the stone one by one, starting with the softest. As long as a point leaves no mark, the stone is harder than it. The first point that scratches it gives the range: here, 6 does not scratch and 7 does, so the stone is between 6 and 7.

steps.title: A destructive test
steps.text: The hardness test is a destructive test: to test, you scratch the stone. So it can be done on a rough stone, or under the base of a cabochon, where nobody will look. It is never done on a cut gem: a scratch on the table or on a facet damages the polish and makes the stone lose its value. When a stone can be identified another way, this test is avoided.

steps.title: To remember
steps.text:
• Hardness measures resistance to scratches.
• Mohs gives the order, absolute hardness gives the gaps.
• Hardness pencils give the range of a stone's hardness.
• It is a destructive test: rough stone or base of a cabochon, never a cut stone.
• A hardness under 7 is a weak point for everyday jewellery.
